facts.claim: "it is what it is" was released as a single by Abe Parker on February 15, 2024. It runs about 3 minutes, and the copyright line is 2024 10K Projects.
The YouTube release credits list Abe Parker as engineer, mixer, producer and vocalist on the track.
Abe Parker is the sole credited songwriter and composer of the song.

The song was later included on the 2024 release 'crawl back to me' (Sept 27, 2024) and on the album 'Phases' (Oct 31, 2025), where it is track 3. An 'unplugged' version came out July 17, 2024. All of these came out through 10K Projects.
The song was also paired with 'numb' on a two-song single released April 18, 2024 on 10K Projects.
Abe Parker is from Blue Rock, Ohio, a small rural town. He moved to Atlanta after college and a season working as a zip line instructor.

Parker has said he is formally trained on guitar. He has written and produced songs for other artists including Marc E Bassy, David Kushner, Lecrae and Crowder, and has accumulated over 16 million streams on his own tracks.

In Atlanta he started by performing on the street and worked his way into clubs such as Smith's Olde Bar and Eddie's Attic. He has opened for acts including Andy Grammer, Judah and the Lion, Ben Rector and David Crowder.
Parker became known through monthly single releases and went viral on TikTok, with songs such as 'Butterflies' and 'Empty House' before the 10K Projects era.

research.lineage: The song sits in the acoustic-leaning indie folk-pop singer-songwriter tradition, with confessional, guitar-driven writing by an Atlanta-based independent artist.

draft:
The title is a shrug, but nothing else in **it is what it is** shrugs. Abe Parker sets the most worn-out phrase in English, the one people use to end a conversation about something that hurts, against a set of verses that refuse to let the matter drop. The narrator is talking to a wall for the echo, running out of alibis, pounding on heaven's gates and hearing nothing back. "It is what it is" is what you say when you've stopped expecting an answer and can't stop asking anyway.

The writing borrows the hymnal's vocabulary and turns it toward doubt. There's a cross carried until the spirit gives out, a soul sent up toward "Heaven's light," a prayer to a Father. The sharpest line inverts a miracle: "You're walking on the water that I'm drowning in." Someone else stands on the surface of the thing that's pulling the narrator under, and the line holds both awe and resentment without picking one. Parker has written for Crowder and Lecrae, and this song speaks their language. It just isn't sure anyone is listening.

What makes it ache is the self-accounting that won't settle. "I lay with someone else's sins" sounds like a complaint about being made to carry another person's damage. Then the bridge flips. The narrator is "the wolf" among the sheep, admits "if I'm the one to blame," and pleads "Father, save me from myself," only to insist, in the same breath, "I didn't choose this hell." Guilt and innocence sit in the same verse, and Parker lets them sit. The last lines turn to a "you" who alone keeps the narrator alive, and that turn is as close to relief as the song gets.

Parker wrote it alone and produced, engineered and mixed it himself, and the sound feels close up. A fingerpicked acoustic pattern carries the song, the guitar of someone who came up playing the street and Atlanta rooms like Eddie's Attic after leaving small-town Blue Rock, Ohio. Kick and snare hold a slow, steady pulse over a plain root-note bass. Parker's voice is breathy and slightly strained, and stacked harmonies gather around it. A synth pad swells while the drums pick up fills and cymbal crashes, then the arrangement pulls back to kick and snare and the pad falls away. That movement is the feeling in miniature: a surge of pleading, then the retreat into resignation.

It's an indie folk-pop song built on a worship song's bones, and the resignation in its title is the thing you say to stop yourself from screaming.

factCheck.claim: The title is a shrug / most worn-out phrase in English, used to end a conversation about something that hurts
factCheck.note: Interpretive framing of the title; stays.

factCheck.claim: Narrator talks to a wall for the echo, is running out of alibis, and pounds heaven's gates with no reply
factCheck.note: Matches lyrics: 'Talking to the wall 'cause, at least, I hear an echo', 'Runnin' out of all these alibis', 'I pound those gates with no reply'.

factCheck.claim: A cross carried until the spirit gives out; soul sent toward 'Heaven's light'; a prayer to a Father
factCheck.note: Imagery is in the lyrics. The 'Heaven's light' quote was turned into a paraphrase to keep within the quotation limit.

factCheck.claim: "You're walking on the water that I'm drowning in."
factCheck.note: Exact lyric. The reading of awe and resentment is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Parker has written for Crowder and Lecrae, and this song speaks their language
factCheck.note: The credit is sourced, but the claim that the song speaks their language is a genre and scene claim the packet doesn't back. Sentence dropped.

factCheck.claim: Then the bridge flips; narrator is "the wolf", admits "if I'm the one to blame" in the bridge, pleads "Father, save me from myself" only to insist "I didn't choose this hell"
factCheck.note: 'If I'm the one to blame' is from an earlier verse, not the section with the wolf. 'I didn't choose this hell' comes before 'Father, save me', not after. 'Bridge' labeling removed. Several fragments paraphrased to stay within the quote limit.

factCheck.claim: The last lines turn to a 'you' who alone keeps the narrator alive
factCheck.note: Lyric: 'But you alone keep me alive'; it appears near the end of the lyric sheet.

factCheck.claim: Parker wrote it alone and produced, engineered and mixed it himself
factCheck.note: Sole songwriter credit; credited as engineer, mixer, producer and vocalist.
Listening notes describe a clean, polished production in a medium-sized room, so 'close up' isn't backed.

factCheck.claim: Fingerpicked acoustic pattern carries the song
factCheck.note: All three passes describe an arpeggiated acoustic guitar, and two say fingerpicked.

factCheck.claim: Parker came up playing the street and Atlanta rooms like Eddie's Attic after leaving small-town Blue Rock, Ohio
factCheck.note: Sourced: from Blue Rock, Ohio, a small rural town; moved to Atlanta; began on the street and worked into clubs like Eddie's Attic. Formal guitar training added from the sourced interview.

factCheck.claim: Kick and snare hold a slow, steady pulse over a plain root-note bass
Breathy, slightly strained voice with stacked harmonies
factCheck.note: Breathy in all passes, strained in two, harmonies in all three.

factCheck.claim: Synth pad swells, drums add fills and cymbal crashes, then pull back to kick and snare and the pad falls away; this is a surge then a retreat
factCheck.note: Elements are backed by passes 2 and 3, but the 'then' sequencing and the surge-then-retreat arc imply position in the song. Reworded without ordering.

factCheck.claim: Indie folk-pop song built on a worship song's bones
factCheck.note: Indie folk-pop is supported by the lineage note; the worship-song claim is not, so it was removed.
